title: Syllables and stress
summary: How to break words into beats, and why the stressed syllable matters
goals: Recognise the four syllable shapes and break words correctly
Know the four stress patterns and the marks that show them
Read the Tagalify sound guide (CAPITALS and ʔ)
Use three handy stress rules for real words

sections.title: Syllables: the beats of a word

blocks.t: A **syllable** is one beat of a word. *ba-sa* has two beats, and *bu-lak-lak* has three. Knowing where the beats fall helps you say each word cleanly.
Tagalog syllables come in **four shapes**. V stands for a vowel and C for a consonant.

Example word
Split into beats

blocks.title: The four shapes
blocks.note: Words often mix shapes. In ak-yat, the first beat is VC and the second is CVC.

blocks.title: The three-sound limit
blocks.t: A syllable never holds more than three sounds, and **ng** counts as one sound. So *ku-mus-ta* (how are you) is split that way, **not** *ku-must-a*. Likewise *pang-a-pat* (fourth) and *ha-ngin* (wind) each keep ng together.

blocks.title: Sound crisp, not breathy
items: Do not puff air after p, t and k. Say them sharply and quietly, as in Spanish.
Avoid long English vowels. Keep them short and pure.
Speak a little faster and sharper than English. A heavy English accent on Tagalog is called a "slang" accent.

sections.title: Stress: the loud part of a word

blocks.t: **Stress** is the syllable you say with extra force. In English, stress rarely changes a word's meaning. In Tagalog it often does.
In books, stress is shown with marks over the vowel. There are **four patterns**.

blocks.title: Four stress patterns
The Tagalify sound guide
items: **CAPITAL letters** show the stressed beat, as in ba-BA-e.
**ʔ** shows the throat stop (glottal catch). It is the tiny closing of the throat between the two halves of "uh-oh".
The throat stop is not a k sound. Beginners often confuse the two.

blocks.title: Why the marks matter
blocks.t: The same letters can be a different word depending on stress. Always learn the stress together with the word. The audio and the sound guide show it.
Say each word aloud, slowly at first, then at normal speed. Tap any word to hear it.

blocks.title: Tap to hear and learn these

blocks.t: Because stress can change meaning, two words can be spelled exactly alike. Listen for the difference.

blocks.title: Pairs to listen for
When in doubt
blocks.t: Context usually tells listeners which word you mean. But wrong stress is one of the most common things that marks a learner, so learn it from the start.
1. The throat stop disappears when an ending is added
When you attach an ending to a word that ends in a throat stop, the stop is dropped and the stress moves.
2. A one-syllable word borrows the stress of the word before it
Short words such as **ka, pa, na, ba, po** do not carry their own stress. The word just before them gives its stress away, so the stress lands on the short word.
3. A hyphen marks the throat stop between a prefix and a root
When a prefix ends in a consonant and the root starts with a vowel, a hyphen keeps them apart and you make a throat stop at the hyphen.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Stress can change meaning, so learn it with every word.
Capitals show stress and ʔ shows the throat stop in the Tagalify guide.
One-syllable words borrow stress from the word before them.

exercises.q: What is the shape of the syllable "an" in an-tay?
exercises.explain: It is a vowel followed by a consonant.

exercises.q: What is the shape of "tak" in tak-bo?
Which is the correct way to split kumusta?
exercises.explain: A syllable never holds more than three sounds.

exercises.q: What is the maximum number of sounds in a Tagalog syllable?
exercises.explain: ng counts as one sound, so pang and ngin both fit.

exercises.q: A grave mark (`) on the last vowel, as in punò, means…
options: Stress on the second-last beat, then a throat stop
exercises.answer: Stress on the second-last beat, then a throat stop
exercises.explain: Grave means next-to-last stress with a glottal catch at the end.

exercises.q: A circumflex (^) on the last vowel, as in punô, means…
options: A quick ending with a throat stop
exercises.answer: A quick ending with a throat stop
exercises.explain: Circumflex means a short end with a glottal stop and no strong stress.

exercises.q: What do CAPITAL letters show in the Tagalify sound guide?
exercises.explain: In ba-BA-e, the capital marks the stressed beat.

exercises.q: What does ʔ show in the sound guide?
options: A tiny stop in the throat
exercises.answer: A tiny stop in the throat
exercises.explain: It is the glottal catch, like the break in uh-oh.

exercises.q: Where does the stress fall in "hin-di PA"?
exercises.explain: A one-syllable word borrows stress from the word before it.

exercises.q: What does the hyphen in pag-asa tell you?
options: Make a throat stop between the prefix and the root
exercises.answer: Make a throat stop between the prefix and the root
exercises.explain: The hyphen separates a consonant-ending prefix from a vowel-starting root.

exercises.q: Which word loses its throat stop when -an is added?
exercises.explain: The final stop disappears and the stress moves.

exercises.q: BU-hay and bu-HAY are spelled the same. What does bu-HAY mean?
exercises.explain: BU-hay is life, and bu-HAY is alive.

recap: Four syllable shapes: V, CV, VC, CVC. No syllable has more than three sounds (ng counts as one).
Four stress patterns: end stress, next-to-last stress, next-to-last with throat stop, quick end with throat stop.
In the Tagalify guide, CAPITALS are the stressed beat and ʔ is the throat stop.
Stress can change meaning, so learn it with every word.
One-syllable words borrow stress. A hyphen marks a throat stop inside a word.
